note: Coding practice that needs no code execution. Import through Questions > Import with format JSON. Subjects and topics are matched by name, so create them first — every name below is offered as a suggested chip when you add the subject, so accepting the suggestions is enough.
howItWorks: CODING and DEBUGGING are graded by you against the author's rubric, which appears only after you commit. OUTPUT_PREDICTION is graded automatically by comparing strings. Nothing here runs code — what PATIPP adds is scheduling the problem to come back and folding the result into your readiness.

questions.subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
questions.stem: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Assume exactly one solution.
questions.explanation: The point of this one is recognising that a single pass with a lookup table beats the obvious nested loop, and being able to say why out loud.

rubric: Solved it in one pass, not two nested loops
Stored values seen so far in a map or object
Said the time and space complexity without being asked
Mentioned what happens if no pair adds up

questions.subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
questions.stem: Reverse a singly linked list in place and return the new head. Do it iteratively.
questions.explanation: Three pointers and an order of operations you have to get exactly right. A classic because it is impossible to fake having done it before.

rubric: Kept hold of the next node before reassigning it
Returned prev, not head, at the end
Handled an empty list and a single node without special cases
Did it in constant extra space

questions.subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
questions.stem: Decide whether a string is a palindrome, ignoring case and anything that is not a letter or digit.
questions.explanation: Easy to get roughly right and easy to get subtly wrong. The two-pointer version avoids allocating a cleaned copy.

rubric: Two pointers rather than building a reversed copy
Skipped non-alphanumeric characters on both sides
Compared case-insensitively
An empty string returns true

questions.subject: JavaScript
questions.stem: Write a debounce function: given a function and a delay, return a wrapper that only invokes it once calls have stopped for that long.
questions.explanation: The question behind the question is whether you understand closures and timer handles. Interviewers ask it because the naive version fails on the second call.

rubric: Held the timer id in a closure, not on the outer scope
Cleared the previous timer before setting a new one
Forwarded both arguments and `this` to the wrapped function
Could explain how debounce differs from throttle

questions.subject: JavaScript
questions.stem: What does this print, and in what order?
questions.explanation: Synchronous code first, then microtasks (promise callbacks), then macrotasks (timers). setTimeout with 0 does not mean immediately — it means after the current task and every queued microtask.

questions.subject: JavaScript
questions.explanation: var is function-scoped, so all three callbacks close over the same binding, which is 3 by the time they run. Changing var to let gives 0 1 2, because let creates a fresh binding per iteration.

questions.subject: JavaScript
questions.explanation: The + operator prefers string concatenation when either side is a string, so 1 + '2' is '12'. The - operator has no string meaning, so '3' is coerced to a number and 12 - 3 is 9.

questions.subject: JavaScript
questions.stem: This should sum the numbers in an array, but it returns NaN. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: The loop condition uses <= so the final iteration reads nums[nums.length], which is undefined. Adding undefined to a number gives NaN, and NaN propagates through the rest of the sum.

payload.defectSummary: The condition should be i < nums.length. With <=, the last iteration reads one index past the end, which is undefined, and adding undefined produces NaN.
rubric: Named it as an off-by-one
Explained why the result is NaN rather than just too large

questions.subject: JavaScript
questions.stem: This is meant to copy a configuration object so the original is untouched. Editing the copy changes the original anyway. Why?
questions.explanation: The spread operator copies one level deep. Nested objects are shared by reference, so mutating copy.database.host also mutates original.database.host.

payload.defectSummary: Spread is a shallow copy. `database` is the same object in both, so writing through the copy writes through the original. A deep copy (structuredClone, or copying each nested object) is needed.
rubric: Said the words shallow copy
Identified that the nested object is shared by reference
Named a way to copy deeply

questions.subject: React
questions.stem: This component fetches on mount, but it re-fetches endlessly. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: The effect has no dependency array, so it runs after every render. It sets state, which causes a render, which runs the effect again. An empty array makes it run once on mount.

payload.defectSummary: The useEffect call has no dependency array, so it runs after every render. It sets state, which triggers a render, which runs the effect again. It should be `}, [id]);` so it re-runs only when id changes.
rubric: Identified the missing dependency array
Explained the set-state-causes-render loop
Chose [id] rather than [] and could say why

questions.subject: React
questions.stem: The button is clicked once. What is logged?
questions.explanation: Both setCount calls read the same `count` from this render's closure, so both compute 0 + 1. The functional form, setCount(c => c + 1), would give 2. The log runs during the same render, before state has updated, so it shows the old value.

questions.subject: React
questions.stem: Write a useDebouncedValue(value, delay) hook that returns the value only after it has stopped changing for the given delay.
questions.explanation: Tests whether you can write a hook with a cleanup function. The cleanup is what most people forget, and without it every keystroke leaves a timer running.

rubric: Returned a cleanup function that clears the timer
Listed both value and delay as dependencies
Initialised state to the current value rather than undefined
Could say why the cleanup matters on every keystroke
